meta.title: The Era of Software Quality, or the Era of Ostriches?
meta.author: calvin

comments.author: pyfisch
comments.text:
Rust will indeed eliminate most memory safety issues (except in unsafe blocks), and you can reasonably expect a Rust project to have an order of magnitude fewer vulnerabilities than a comparable project written in C or C++ or Vala.



Currently the best solution is to not use programming language package managers, but GNOME’s Rust code depends heavily on Cargo. Accordingly, I recommend against using Rust for writing GNOME software.


In my opinion the response should be to pin versions of the dependencies or fork and maintain them in the GNOME project, rather than avoiding a programming language the author claims reduces vulnerabilities by an order of magnitude.

comments.author: wrs
comments.text: The author seems to conflate “using programming language package managers” with “having uncontrolled dependencies”, which I don’t think is valid. I’m pretty sure you could configure a Rust build with controlled dependencies. (And a C++ build with uncontrolled ones.)

comments.author: ghoti
comments.text: Rust has no inherent coupling to Cargo. Rust codebases can be built with make, cmake, or any other build system by directly invoking rustc in the same manner one would directly invoke gcc. For Rust projects whose build system is Cargo, the cargo vendor subcommand conveniently produces a vendored tree of dependencies amenable to version control.

comments.author: wrs
comments.text:
Right. I suspect what the author meant was more like “you can’t write a useful Rust program without using lots of external packages”. A comment on the ecosystem, not the language.

Of course, you could also say “you can’t write a useful C++ program without reinventing a bunch of wheels insecurely”.

comments.author: abrambleninja
comments.text:
I'm a big Rust enthusiast but I think that metric misses the point for this particular discussion. For supply chain vulnerabilities, I think that number of unique packages (or perhaps more accurate would be number of unique package authors) is the most important metric, because if you are an outsider trying to perform a supply chain attack, you are looking to compromise any single package in the dependency tree of your target.

I think the LoC or bytes metrics are definitely relevant when discussing bloat of a library or application, and I get a bit irked when I see the number of Cargo packages being pulled in as an argument about that, but in the supply chain case I do think it is unfortunately quite relevant.

I don't have a good solution to this besides automated scanning of crates published, as well as a cooldown period in Cargo (or one of the wrappers or crate mirrors that provides this), but it still feels incomplete to me.

comments.author: kingmob
comments.text:
People love to cite "appeal to authority" whenever an expert disagrees with them, as if it magically negates their expertise. But unless you can prove someone is NOT an expert despite having credentials/title/position/etc, their "authority" is a relevant shorthand for expertise. From a classical logic perspective, this is not true, but classical logic is simplistic. From a Bayesian perspective, authority should usefully update one's priors.

Regardless, you provided even less justification for your assessment of the author, so it's not like you have a logically better argument. There's not even an argument there, just an assertion.


I know we're being snarky, but I'll respond to the nuance bit as if it were real. Nuance doesn't mean we can't write quality software without LLMs, but if we're up-to-date on current LLM capabilities, we have to admit they can do a lot of what they say on the tin. In some areas, like debugging and security, they're already better or faster than most human devs. Any argument that starts off assuming LLMs don't work in any scenario, is either naive or out-of-date.

A nuanced argument involves looking at them and deciding how to handle the trade-offs instead. How do we enable junior devs to grow? How to we triage large numbers of issues/PRs? How do we compensate for LLMs' (currently) weak high-level architectural design? How do I balance learning with throughput, so my skills don't atrophy? Which skills are still relevant? Etc.

comments.author: gunduzc
comments.text:
I guess this is where I should drop the snark and tell you that my attitude towards this discussion isn't purely grounded in technical terms. In an idealized environment where LLMs have no adverse impact on the world they reside in, a developer can write code by hand, iterate until they can't see an issue, and only then ask an LLM for a review. This evades a lot of the "technical" problems with LLM usage at a slight cost of development time. More importantly, it works.

I just think it's especially ironic to make the claim "there is no way to write quality software without LLM use".

I never for a second considered GNOME, Epiphany, GLib, WebKit, Fedora in general to be "quality software". Quality software acknowledges that being readable is more important than having been written. Quality software is Lua, it's TCC, it's NetBSD, it's Guix. And none of them required an LLM touch.

From what I've seen, Red Hat has never cared if people that are not their engineers can read their source code. (In fact, you may remember that they actively tried to close the sources of their operating systems.) Red Hat has no stronger incentive to create quality software than Microsoft does.

So no, I could not disagree more with the author about what "quality software" is. And hearing the author say "no quality software without stochastic parrot" is funny, because I think the author wouldn't know quality software if it kicked down their door and announced it was suing Red Hat for impersonation.

I have no technical basis of rejecting LLMs altogether. The right open weights model may or may not be able to outperform your average developer, but there is no question if it would help when it's used alongside a human brain (rather than as a substitute for one).

I have a cultural basis of rejecting them and objecting to them. LLMs are marketed as a way to replace developers, not make their lives easier. LLMs are not our friend, they exist so that we get paid less. In my opinion, no discussion that overlooks this or discounts this can be "nuanced". And in my opinion, this one didn't even get close to nuance.

Most importantly, there is absolutely no nuance in stating "you either agree with me, or you're unserious or delusional". Who does the author think they are? Jesus Christ? Anakin Skywalker? "Either you're with me, or you're my enemy"? Where's the nuance in that?

comments.author: kornel
comments.text:
Unsafe languages need to deal with all the same high-level bugs (like access control or SQL injection) in addition to memory safety bugs. C is not trading memory unsafety for some other safety, it's strictly more unsafe.
Rust does a lot to prevent logic bugs, e.g. error handling can be enforced by the compiler, while C can't even decide whether returning 0 means OK or false.




Memory unsafety vulnerabilities are exceptional in their unbound scope and severity.



Without arbitrary code execution, the danger is roughly limited to what the code is supposed to do, and plenty of programs have lots of boring code that doesn't touch anything sensitive. Even if you're implementing access control, the worst case without RCE is failing open on that endpoint, rather than enabling installation of a rootkit or such.

A memory-safe JSON parser can at worst give you garbage data or heat your CPU or eat your RAM, but it won't run arbitrary attacker-supplied code. If you're implementing a widget that queries the current weather, the the worst case is not getting the weather info. In C, the worst case is getting the whole system pwned through a weather info widget. It's a massive difference in the attack surface.

That still fits under "the danger is roughly limited to what the code is supposed to do". But you're missing the point that in C you don't need an API for RCE get RCE. In C you have a much larger problem of memory unsafety and UB turning potentially any API into an arbitrary code execution gadget.

comments.author: skyfaller
comments.text:
There is some very strange cognitive dissonance in your comment. On the one hand, you say that efficiency will solve the climate impact of LLMs. On the other hand, you recognize that efficiency won't solve the climate impact, in the same comment! You handwave the problem with efficiency away by blaming it on capitalism, but who cares why efficiency doesn't work if you've just invalidated your own solution?

For those not familiar, we're discussing the Jevons Paradox, which says as we make a technology more efficient, we use it more, thereby increasing use of resources. I recently saw a fantastic framing of the Jevons Paradox:


Making use of a resource more profitable increases the return on investment of exploiting that resource.

So increased systems efficiency increases, not decreases, resource use.

Unless your approach is to have a fixed expectation for capability and just optimize for lower and lower resource use to achieve that capability. Which is not how capitalism works, at all.


I agree that this problem is almost impossible to solve under capitalism, capitalism needs to go, but let's be fair, it's still a very difficult problem for any alternative economic system. I'd say we should reject any alternative economic system if it doesn't have some answer for this formulation of the Jevons Paradox; it seems like a good test for whether it can handle existential threats like the climate crisis.

comments.author: kingmob
comments.text:
Ahh, the "dissonance" is you're thinking of the Jevons Paradox as being about increased energy use, when it's more specifically about the increased usage of goods and services, not necessarily energy.

You're on the right track, but e.g., if LLM use increased 10x, but we're able to make them 20x more efficient, the energy use will drop, despite Jevons. Alternatively, Jevons could drive 20x more carbon-neutral solar/wind development making the increased energy use of LLMs (and everything else) a moot point. This is what I think (and hope) will happen, even under capitalism.


It's unclear to me that the Jevons Paradox would be as much of a problem under other economic systems. To use its original observation about coal: yes, ordinary citizens would continue to want coal and electricity, but much of the usage was by capitalist-driven industry.  Companies had to use more coal to ensure they weren't out-competed by those who did.

A more democratic economic system could weigh the trade-offs, and voters could decide how quickly and how much to adopt a new tech.

comments.author: schneems
comments.text:
I’m trying to contribute to clippy now and the situation looks bleak for maintainers.

Previously the signal was: could make a PR. Things like docs and tests were "wow this person is good" and a description that linked to the issue it closes and actually explained that it did was a 10/10.

Mantainers have always relied on signals to determine where to invest their limited time. When they do invest it, it was clear their empathy is met and reciprocated. Now those signals are gone and there's not a good way to distinguish between "I spent days and hours meticulously promoting fans getting reviews and iterating combined with my own human iteration" and "told Claude to get me internet points to boost my resume in a Ralph loop". There's not even a guarantee the person on the other side is in fact a person.

The rust/clippy policy is very thoughtful and clearly spells out how to use LLMs with empathy for the eventual maintainer/reviewer. I ran afoul of it by some degrees and even though I'm in the "meticulous code" camp of LLM users cannot genuinely say code produced by the machine isn't in the final product. I can though, and will. So closed it and will rewrite it.

I think LLM scanning is good. But LLM issues and PRs are not. We need a human who has the skills and empathy for reviewers to make it easy enough for them. The challenge has never been the work, the challenge has always been doing the work in a way that is reviewable, maintainable, and sustainable. We need to find community standards and guidelines to reflect that reality.

I think the empathy gap is challenging here. At this point, people have a different sense of how important code is. Some people have gotten really used to shipping products quickly. Friction is anathema to them.

For some work projects, I found myself writing detailed replies to some PRs only to have them answered immediately. That indicated to me that the person didn't even read what I wrote. They just told Claude, "hey, there is a reply. Go handle it."

I fear that approaching an overwhelming onslaught of automated contributions with empathy is just fuel for burn out.

comments.author: frontsideair
comments.text:
That's the part I'm most bothered about. I agree with the "Vulnerability reporting is a public service, not an obligation" part, but it's not a binary choice, it's not the reporter either reports with slop or doesn't report at all.

A better solution is that the reporter only reports the existence of the vulnerability, and the prompt they used, if they don't feel like writing a report themselves. Then the maintainer can either check themselves, or point their agent to it if they want to. Since basically everyone has access to a frontier agent, why submit the build artifact?

I think this works better than slop reports, because AI is becoming infectious. The reports are so impenetrable to humans, you end up having to use an agent yourself. But it doesn't have to be this way. And if the reporter can bother to distill the report to a human-made version, all the better for everyone involved!

comments.author: motet-a

Accordingly, I recommend against using Rust for writing GNOME software.

I don't think you do agree with me.


The problems with the quality of our software were there all along.


You could make the same argument concerning any system designed to live in an equilibrium with the environment it was created for. I wouldn't say cities built by the coast are poor quality, or had problems that were there all along, because they do not have flood defences, even if it is now becoming a major problem due to a shifting climate.

I don't mean to say that you are wrong for being glad we are finding vulnerabilities, perhaps it leads to a better place. I hope however you can understand that I feel sad about it, as I feel that the benefits we see from these things are  outweighed by the negative externalities of their existence and widespread adoption, in a similar way to how the delicious wine we can now grow in my country is not worth the externalities of the climate crisis.

comments.author: bediger4000
comments.text: I hate that the author is correct: AI-generated bug reports have that weird jargon about "gated" array access, every version or test is "pinned", every test case is a "fixture". Between the omnijargon and the meandering sentences, I'm always about half certain that any given bug report is nonsense. But this article does explain the tension between real, albeit exotic issues and figuring out inhuman verbiage.
